concepts.name: nth term of a GP
concepts.description: The nth term is the first term multiplied by the common ratio, (n − 1) times.

concepts.name: Sum of a finite GP
concepts.description: The sum of the first n terms has a direct formula in terms of the first term, ratio and n.

concepts.name: Sum to infinity
concepts.description: When the common ratio is a proper fraction, the sum of infinitely many terms converges to a finite value.

concepts.name: Finding the common ratio
concepts.description: Divide any term by the one before it, or use two known terms to solve for the ratio.

concepts.name: Geometric mean
concepts.description: The geometric mean of two numbers is the middle term that keeps them in a three-term GP.

formulas.title: nth term of a GP
formulas.prompt: What is the formula for the nth term of a GP?
formulas.explanation: a is the first term and r is the common ratio; the exponent is (n − 1), not n.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the 5th term of a GP with a = 3 and r = 2.

formulas.title: Sum of the first n terms
formulas.prompt: What is the formula for the sum of the first n terms of a GP?
formulas.explanation: This adds up n terms directly without listing and adding each one.
formulas.commonMistake: Using rⁿ instead of r^(n−1) inside the formula, or forgetting to subtract 1.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the sum of the first 5 terms of a GP with a = 2 and r = 3.

formulas.title: Sum to infinity
formulas.prompt: When does a GP have a finite sum to infinity, and what is it?
formulas.formula: S∞ = a / (1 − r),  valid only when |r| < 1
formulas.explanation: If |r| ≥ 1, the terms do not shrink to zero, so the sum grows without bound and has no finite value.
formulas.commonMistake: Applying the formula when |r| ≥ 1, where it does not apply.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the sum to infinity of a GP with a = 8 and r = 1/2.

formulas.title: Finding the common ratio
formulas.prompt: How do you find r from two known terms of a GP?
formulas.formula: If Tm and Tk are known terms with m > k, then r^(m − k) = Tm / Tk
formulas.explanation: Take the ratio of the two terms, then undo the exponent to isolate r.
formulas.commonMistake: Dividing the terms without accounting for how many steps apart they are.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find r given T1 = 5 and T4 = 135.

formulas.title: Geometric mean
formulas.prompt: What is the geometric mean of two numbers a and b, and how does it relate to a GP?
formulas.formula: Geometric mean G = √(ab); for three terms a, G, b in GP, G² = ab
formulas.explanation: The geometric mean is the number that keeps the three terms in a constant ratio.
formulas.commonMistake: Computing the arithmetic mean (a + b)/2 instead of the geometric mean.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the geometric mean of 4 and 16.

formulas.title: Three unknown terms in a GP
formulas.prompt: How do you pick three unknown terms of a GP to make the algebra easy?
formulas.formula:
Write them a/r, a, ar
Their product is a³, and b² = ac for terms a, b, c
formulas.explanation: With the middle term as a, the product loses r completely.
formulas.example: Three GP terms with product 216 and sum 19: middle = ∛216 = 6, then 6/r + 6 + 6r = 19 gives r = 3/2: 4, 6, 9.
formulas.commonMistake: Writing a, ar, ar², which keeps r in the product.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Three numbers in GP multiply to 64 and add to 14.

formulas.title: Recurring decimals are GP sums
formulas.formula:
0.aaa… = a/9
0.abab… = ab/99
(a GP: first term a/10, ratio 1/10)
formulas.explanation: Each repeat adds a tenth (or hundredth) of the previous one, and a/(1 − r) gives the exact sum.
formulas.commonMistake: Using 100 instead of 99 in the denominator.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Write 0.272727… as a fraction in lowest terms.

levels.title: Multiplying by the Same Ratio
levels.description: A sequence where each term is the last one multiplied by a constant ratio.

blocks.title: What makes a GP
blocks.body: In 2, 6, 18, 54, each term is 3 times the one before it. That constant multiplier, 3, is the common ratio r, and it defines the whole sequence together with the first term.

blocks.title: nth term
blocks.caption: The exponent is one less than the term number.

blocks.body: Find r by dividing any term by the one right before it.

levels.title: Geometric Progression Formulas
levels.description: nth term, sum of n terms, sum to infinity, finding the ratio, geometric mean.

levels.title: Direct Terms and Ratios
levels.description: Finding terms, ratios and the geometric mean directly.

levels.title: Sums and Reverse Problems
levels.description: Summing a GP, and working backwards from a term to find a or r.

levels.title: Applied Geometric Progression
levels.description: Multi-step problems combining several GP ideas.

questions.question: A GP has first term 3 and common ratio 2. What is the 5th term?

hints.text: The exponent for the 5th term is 4, not 5.

questions.question: The first two terms of a GP are 4 and 12. What is the common ratio?
questions.method: Divide a term by the one before it.

hints.text: The ratio is found by dividing consecutive terms.

questions.question: The sum-to-infinity formula S∞ = a/(1 − r) only gives a finite value when
questions.explanation: If |r| ≥ 1, the terms do not shrink towards zero, so the sum never settles to a finite value.
questions.method: The condition is on the size of r, not its sign or a.

hints.text: Think about what happens to the terms if r = 2.

questions.question: What is the geometric mean of 4 and 16?
questions.method: Take the square root of the product.

hints.text: This is not the same as the average (arithmetic mean).

questions.question: What comes next: 2, 6, 18, 54, ?
questions.explanation: The common ratio is 3, so the next term is 54 × 3 = 162.
questions.method: Multiply the last term by the common ratio.

hints.text: Check the ratio between consecutive terms first.

commonMistakes: Adding a fixed amount instead of multiplying.

questions.question: What is the sum of the first 5 terms of a GP with first term 2 and common ratio 3?
What is the sum to infinity of a GP with first term 8 and common ratio 1/2?
questions.method: Divide the first term by (1 − r).

hints.text: Dividing by 1/2 is the same as multiplying by 2.

commonMistakes: Multiplying by (1 − r) instead of dividing.

questions.question: A GP has first term 5 and 4th term 135. What is the common ratio?
questions.explanation: T4 = a·r³, so 135 = 5r³, giving r³ = 27, so r = 3.
questions.method: Set up Tn = a·r^(n−1) and solve for r.

hints.text: The exponent for the 4th term is 3.

questions.question: A GP has common ratio 2 and 6th term 192. What is the first term?
questions.method: Substitute into Tn = a·r^(n−1) and solve for a.

hints.text: The exponent for the 6th term is 5.

questions.question: A ball is dropped and each bounce reaches 60% of the height of the previous bounce. If the first bounce reaches 60 m, what is the total height of all the bounces added together (to infinity)?
questions.method: Model the bounce heights as a GP and apply the sum-to-infinity formula.
commonMistakes: Using the initial drop height as the first term instead of the first bounce.

questions.question: A GP has first term 3 and common ratio 2. Which term of the sequence equals 384?
questions.method: Express both sides as powers of the same base.

hints.text: Divide 384 by the first term before comparing powers of 2.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to add 1 back after finding the exponent.

questions.question: Three numbers in GP have a sum of 26 and a product of 216. What is the middle term?
questions.explanation: For three terms in GP, the product equals the cube of the middle term: middle³ = 216, so middle = 6. (This is consistent with a sum of 26: the other two terms are 6/3 = 2 and 6×3 = 18, summing to 26 with ratio 3.)
solutionSteps: For a, G, b in GP: a×G×b = G³.
questions.method: The product of three GP terms is the cube of the middle term.

hints.text: You do not need the sum to find the middle term from the product.

commonMistakes: Trying to use the sum before realising the product alone determines the middle term.

questions.question: A ball is dropped from 100 m. Each time it bounces, it rises to 1/5 of the height it fell from, and this continues forever. What is the total distance travelled by the ball (counting every fall and every rise)?
questions.explanation: The bounce heights form a GP with a = 100/5 = 20 and r = 1/5, so their sum is 20/(1 − 1/5) = 25. Each bounce height is travelled twice (up and down), so the total distance is the initial 100 m drop plus 2 × 25 = 150 m.
solutionSteps: Each bounce is travelled up and down: 2 × 25 = 50.
questions.method: Sum the bounce heights first, then double them for up-and-down travel, and add the initial drop.

hints.text: Every bounce height is travelled twice: once up, once down.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to double the bounce heights, or forgetting to add the initial drop.
